etymology: Old English feawe; Webster (1828) sets it beside Latin pauci, noting that “the senses of few and small are often united.” In the Gospels it renders Greek oligos (G3641), little or small in number.
biblical_def: Few is one of the hardest words Christ ever spoke, and He spoke it on purpose. At the close of the Sermon on the Mount He set two gates before His hearers: “Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat” (Mat 7:13), and then: “Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it” (Mat 7:14). When a man asked Him outright, “Lord, are there few that be saved?” (Luk 13:23), He did not soften the number; He told the questioner to strive to enter. The parable of the wedding feast closes on the same note: “For many are called, but few are chosen” (Mat 22:14). The general call of the gospel goes out to all who hear it; the effectual call reaches the elect, and they come. Peter finds the pattern already in the flood, where “few, that is, eight souls were saved by water” (1Pe 3:20). The word does not make God stingy. It makes the way narrow, and it makes the question personal: not how many will be saved, but whether you have entered.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): FEW, not many; small in number.
webster_full: FEW, adjective [Latin pauci. The senses of few and small are often united.]
Not many; small in number.
Party is the madness of many for the gain of a few; but few men, in times of party, regard the maxim.
scriptures: Mat 7:14
Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.
For many are called, but few are chosen.
Then said one unto him, Lord, are there few that be saved? And he said unto them,
Which sometime were disobedient, when once the longsuffering of God waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was a preparing, wherein few, that is, eight souls were saved by water.
corruption_summary: The modern pulpit treats Christ's “few” as an embarrassment to be explained away, either by quietly assuming nearly everyone is saved or by measuring faithfulness by crowd size.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors meet at this word. The first is the soft universalism of the age, which cannot bear a narrow gate and so assumes, without ever saying it aloud, that the way to life is in practice wide. Christ answered that assumption before it was made: many go in at the broad gate, and few find the narrow one. To preach as though the proportion were reversed is to contradict the Lord in His own sermon.

The second error runs the other way and is just as worldly: it takes the size of a gathering as proof of God's blessing. The flood, the remnant in Elijah's day and the eight souls in the ark all say otherwise. The church does not choose between many and few; it preaches the gate, calls every hearer to strive to enter, and leaves the number to the God who chose His people before the foundation of the world.
roots_summary: English few, Latin pauci; Greek oligos (G3641), the word Christ used at the narrow gate.
roots_lines: Greek oligos (G3641), little, few, small in number.
Tagged at Mat 7:14, Mat 22:14 and 1Pe 3:20 in the Authorized Version.
Webster ties few to small: the senses are often united.
The narrow gate and the broad gate are set side by side in Mat 7:13-14.
Eight souls in the ark are Peter's picture of the few.
usage: few there be that find it
names the small number who enter the narrow gate
set against the many on the broad way

pos: adv. / adj. (to a greater distance; additional)
etymology: Old English furthor, from forth. Webster (1828) gives it as adjective (more distant; additional), adverb (to a greater distance) and verb (to help forward). In the Authorized Version it renders several originals, among them Hebrew yasaph (H3254), to add, and Greek epi (G1909) in the phrase “no further.”
biblical_def: Scripture uses further most memorably to mark a line that God draws and no one crosses. Out of the whirlwind the LORD tells Job how He set bounds for the sea: “Hitherto shalt thou come, but no further: and here shall thy proud waves be stayed?” (Job 38:11). The ocean goes exactly as far as it is told. The same limit holds over every enemy of the truth. When the council wanted the name of Jesus silenced they said, “But that it spread no further among the people, let us straitly threaten them” (Act 4:17), and it spread to the ends of the earth. Paul says of the false teachers of the last days, “But they shall proceed no further: for their folly shall be manifest unto all men” (2Ti 3:9). The one place in the Gospels where someone goes further than anyone could follow is Gethsemane: “And he went a little further, and fell on his face, and prayed” (Mat 26:39). There Christ went the distance alone that His people could not go, and drank the cup they could not drink. Further is the word of God's limits and of Christ's lone obedience.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): FURTHER, more distant; additional; to a greater distance; to help forward.
webster_full: FUR'THER, adjective 1. More or most distant; as the further end of the field.
2. Additional. We have a further reason for this opinion. We have nothing further to suggest.
FUR'THER, adverb To a greater distance. He went further.
FUR'THER, verb transitive To help forward; to promote; to advance onward; to forward; hence, to help or assist.
scriptures: And said, Hitherto shalt thou come, but no further: and here shall thy proud waves be stayed?
Act 4:17
But that it spread no further among the people, let us straitly threaten them, that they speak henceforth to no man in this name.
But they shall proceed no further: for their folly shall be manifest unto all men, as theirs also was.
And he went a little further, and fell on his face, and prayed, saying, O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.
corruption_summary: The age treats every limit as an insult to be pushed past, while Scripture teaches that God sets the bound and says “no further.”
corruption_paragraphs: Modern progressivism, in the church and out of it, measures virtue by how far one has moved beyond the old boundaries. Each generation is praised for going further than the last, and Scripture itself is treated as a starting line rather than a fence. Job 38 answers that spirit at its root: the proud waves are stayed where God speaks, and the creature that cannot command the sea does not get to redraw the bounds of the moral law.

The same word comforts the church under pressure. Threats against the gospel and the spread of error both meet a limit they did not set. The council could not stop the name from spreading; the deceivers of 2 Timothy 3 proceed no further than God allows before their folly is manifest. God's providence is not a theory here but a promise.
roots_summary: English further, from forth; Hebrew yasaph (H3254), to add; Greek epi (G1909) in “no further.”
roots_lines: Hebrew yasaph (H3254), to add, tagged at Job 38:11.
Greek epi (G1909), tagged at Act 4:17 and 2Ti 3:9.

usage: Hitherto shalt thou come, but no further
marks the bound God sets on sea, enemy and error alike
and the distance Christ went alone in Gethsemane

pos: n. (malice; ill will with a desire to vex)
etymology: Middle English spite, shortened from despite. At Psalm 10:14 it renders Hebrew ka’as (H3708), vexation or provocation.
biblical_def: Psalm 10 is the cry of the poor man while the wicked prosper. The wicked man says in his heart that God has forgotten, that He hides His face and will never see it. The psalmist answers him directly: “Thou hast seen it; for thou beholdest mischief and spite, to requite it with thy hand: the poor committeth himself unto thee; thou art the helper of the fatherless” (Psa 10:14). Spite is the small, deliberate cruelty that wants to vex its victim, the provocation that counts on going unnoticed. The verse says three things about it. God sees it, every instance. God will requite it with His own hand, so the injured man need not. And the poor man therefore commits himself to God instead of to revenge. Paul builds on the same ground: “Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord” (Rom 12:19). Christ is the pattern, “who, when he was reviled, reviled not again… but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously” (1Pe 2:23). The answer to spite is not more spite, and not silence about wrong, but a hand placed in God's.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): SPITE, hatred; rancor; malice; often a sudden fit of ill will, with a desire to vex.
webster_full: SPITE, noun Hatred; rancor; malice; malignity; malevolence.

SPITE, however, is not always synonymous with these words. It often denotes a less deliberate and fixed hatred than malice and malignity, and is often a sudden fit of ill will excited by temporary vexation.
It is the effect of extreme irritation, and is accompanied with a desire of revenge, or at least a desire to vex the object of ill will.
In spite of, in opposition to all efforts; in defiance or contempt of.
SPITE, verb transitive 1. To be angry or vexed at. 2. To mischief; to vex; to treat maliciously; to thwart.
scriptures: Thou hast seen it; for thou beholdest mischief and spite, to requite it with thy hand: the poor committeth himself unto thee; thou art the helper of the fatherless.
Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.
Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously:
corruption_summary: Spite is rebranded as justified pushback, and the culture of grievance trains people to answer every slight in kind instead of committing the wrong to God.
corruption_paragraphs: Online life has made spite a public sport. The wounding remark, the pile-on and the act of revenge are celebrated as standing up for oneself, and the person who declines to retaliate is called weak. Webster's definition fits the age exactly: ill will excited by temporary vexation and accompanied with a desire to vex. What the age calls strength, Scripture calls the flesh.

Psalm 10 does not ask the afflicted to pretend nothing happened. It names the mischief and spite, and it insists that God has seen it and will requite it. That is what frees the believer from vengeance: the account is not dropped but transferred to the Judge. Romans 12 and 1 Peter 2 make the same transfer, and both rest it on the character of God, not on the merit of the offender.
roots_summary: From despite; Hebrew ka’as (H3708), vexation, provocation, at Psalm 10:14.
roots_lines: Hebrew ka'as (H3708), vexation, grief, provocation, tagged at Psa 10:14.
English spite is a shortened form of despite.
Webster distinguishes spite from settled malice: a sudden fit of ill will.
Psalm 10:14 is the only occurrence of spite in the Authorized Version.
The adverb spitefully appears in the Gospels for the abuse of Christ.
usage: thou beholdest mischief and spite
names the petty cruelty that wants to vex and expects to go unseen
answered by God's sight and God's hand, not by revenge

etymology: From stead, a place or standing. Webster (1828) spells the word steddy and defines the verb as “to hold or keep from shaking, reeling or falling; to support; to make or keep firm.”
biblical_def: The single occurrence of steady in the Authorized Version comes from the battle with Amalek at Rephidim. Joshua fought in the valley while Moses stood on the hill with the rod of God, and the outcome followed his hands: “And it came to pass, when Moses held up his hand, that Israel prevailed: and when he let down his hand, Amalek prevailed” (Exo 17:11). Moses grew tired, as men do. “But Moses' hands were heavy; and they took a stone, and put it under him, and he sat thereon; and Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands, the one on the one side, and the other on the other side; and his hands were steady until the going down of the sun” (Exo 17:12). The steadiness was not Moses' own. It came from a stone beneath him and two men beside him. That is the picture of perseverance in the church: no saint holds up his hands alone, and the means God provides, His Word, His people and their prayers, keep weak hands steady until the day is done. Hebrews gives the charge to every congregation: “Wherefore lift up the hands which hang down, and the feeble knees” (Heb 12:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828), under STEDDY: to hold or keep from shaking, reeling or falling; to support; to make or keep firm.
webster_full: STEDDY, verb transitive To hold or keep from shaking, reeling or falling; to support; to make or keep firm.
STEDDY my hand.
scriptures: And it came to pass, when Moses held up his hand, that Israel prevailed: and when he let down his hand, Amalek prevailed.

But Moses' hands were heavy; and they took a stone, and put it under him, and he sat thereon; and Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands, the one on the one side, and the other on the other side; and his hands were steady until the going down of the sun.
Wherefore lift up the hands which hang down, and the feeble knees;
corruption_summary: Steadiness is sold as self-made resilience, an inner resource cultivated alone, when Scripture shows it as a gift held up by God's means and God's people.
corruption_paragraphs: The self-help industry and its church imitators teach that the steady person is the one who has built enough inner strength, discipline and mindset to need no one. Exodus 17 says the opposite. Moses' hands were heavy. They were steady only because a stone was set beneath him and Aaron and Hur stood on either side. Perseverance is real, but it is upheld, not self-generated.

This also corrects a lonely individualism that treats the local church as optional. The man who will not be helped by the ordinary means of grace, the preaching of the Word, the fellowship of the saints and their prayers, has chosen to hold up his own hands. Hebrews 12:12 is addressed to a congregation, and the hands it tells them to lift are each other's.
roots_summary: From stead, a standing place; Webster's steddy, to keep from shaking; Exodus 17:12 is the only occurrence.
roots_lines: English steady, from stead, a place or standing.
Webster (1828) spells it steddy and defines the verb: to keep firm.
Exo 17:12 is the only occurrence of steady in the Authorized Version.
Aaron and Hur stayed up Moses' hands, one on each side.
Related forms in the dictionary: steadfast, steadiness.
usage: his hands were steady until the going down of the sun
describes firmness held up by God's provision and by brethren
rather than strength produced alone

pos: v. intr. (to gaze with fixed, wide-open eyes)
etymology: Old English starian. Webster (1828) connects it with words of stiffness and tension: “to look with fixed eyes wide open.” At Psalm 22:17 it renders Hebrew ra’ah (H7200), to see.
biblical_def: Stare appears once in the Authorized Version, in the psalm Christ quoted from the cross. Psalm 22 opens with “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” and goes on to describe a death by exposure in startling detail: “For dogs have compassed me: the assembly of the wicked have inclosed me: they pierced my hands and my feet” (Psa 22:16), and then, “I may tell all my bones: they look and stare upon me” (Psa 22:17). The sufferer is stripped and stretched so that every bone can be counted, and the crowd does not look away. It gazes. The Gospels record the fulfilment without comment: “And the people stood beholding. And the rulers also with them derided him” (Luk 23:35). The stare is part of the shame Christ bore. He was made a spectacle, endured the open gaze of His enemies and the curiosity of the idle, and despised the shame for the joy set before Him. Every believer who has been looked at with contempt for His name should remember that the Lord was stared at first.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): STARE, to gaze; to look with fixed eyes wide open; to fasten an earnest look on some object.
webster_full: STARE, verb intransitive 1. To gaze; to look with fixed eyes wide open; to fasten an earnest look on some object.
Staring is produced by wonder, surprise, stupidity, horror, fright and sometimes by eagerness to hear or learn something, sometimes by impudence.
We say, he stared with astonishment.
To stare in the face, to be before the eyes or undeniably evident.
STARE, noun A fixed look with eyes wide open.
scriptures: I may tell all my bones: they look and stare upon me.
For dogs have compassed me: the assembly of the wicked have inclosed me: they pierced my hands and my feet.
And the people stood beholding. And the rulers also with them derided him, saying, He saved others; let him save himself, if he be Christ, the chosen of God.
corruption_summary: Critical scholarship strips Psalm 22 of its prophecy, treating the staring crowd as generic lament imagery rather than a prediction fulfilled at Calvary.
corruption_paragraphs: Historical-critical commentary has long read Psalm 22 as an anonymous sufferer's lament whose correspondence with the crucifixion is coincidence, or the result of Gospel writers shaping their story to fit the psalm. Both moves deny what the New Testament plainly claims: that David, being a prophet, spoke of the sufferings of Christ. The pierced hands and feet, the parted garments and the staring crowd are not literary borrowing but fulfilled prediction.

The word also exposes the spectator's sin. The crowd at the cross did not join the mockery of the rulers in every case; some only watched. Scripture does not count that neutrality as innocence. To stare at Christ crucified and remain unmoved is still to stand with those who gazed and went home.
roots_summary: Old English starian; Hebrew ra’ah (H7200), to see, at Psalm 22:17.
roots_lines: Hebrew ra'ah (H7200), to see, tagged at Psa 22:17.
Webster: to look with fixed eyes wide open.
Psa 22:17 is the only occurrence of stare in the Authorized Version.
Christ quoted the opening of Psalm 22 from the cross.
Luk 23:35 records the people standing and beholding.
usage: they look and stare upon me
names the open gaze of the crowd at the crucified Christ
part of the shame He bore for His people

etymology: From move with the suffix -able. Webster (1828) spells it movable: “that may or does change from one time to another.” At Proverbs 5:6 it renders Hebrew nua (H5128), to wander or totter.
biblical_def: Proverbs 5 is a father's warning to his son about the strange woman. She does not look dangerous: “For the lips of a strange woman drop as an honeycomb, and her mouth is smoother than oil” (Pro 5:3). The father then describes her path in one striking word: “Lest thou shouldest ponder the path of life, her ways are moveable, that thou canst not know them” (Pro 5:6). Her ways wander. They shift so that no one can map them, and they are designed to keep a young man from stopping to consider where he is going. Adultery depends on that: it never lets its victim see the end of the road from the beginning. Against her wandering ways Proverbs sets a fixed point that does not move: “For the ways of man are before the eyes of the LORD, and he pondereth all his goings” (Pro 5:21). The son is told to ponder his path because God ponders it. Wisdom is a path that stays where it is; sin keeps moving the ground under your feet.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), under MOVABLE: that may be moved; that may or does change from one time to another.
webster_full: MOVABLE, adjective [from move.] That may be moved; that can or may be lifted, carried, drawn, turned or conveyed, or in any way made to change place or posture; susceptible of motion.
1. That may or does change from one time to another; as a movable feast.
A movable letter, in Hebrew grammar, is one that is pronounced, as opposed to one that is quiescent.
scriptures: Pro 5:6
Lest thou shouldest ponder the path of life, her ways are moveable, that thou canst not know them.
Pro 5:3
For the lips of a strange woman drop as an honeycomb, and her mouth is smoother than oil:
Pro 5:21
For the ways of man are before the eyes of the LORD, and he pondereth all his goings.
corruption_summary: Moving moral ground is praised as growth and authenticity, when Proverbs shows shifting ways as the mark of the strange woman's path.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern ethic prizes fluidity: identities, commitments and even marriage vows are expected to shift as the self evolves, and to hold a fixed standard is called rigid. Proverbs 5 describes that fluidity and gives it a name. Her ways are moveable so that thou canst not know them. Shifting ground is not a sign of wisdom but the strategy of seduction, because a path that keeps moving can never be judged by where it ends.

Against that, the father sets a God who ponders all a man's goings. The moral law does not move with the culture, and neither does the covenant of marriage. A son who learns to ponder the path of life, rather than drift on smooth words, is learning the fear of the LORD.
roots_summary: From move; Webster's movable; Hebrew nua (H5128), to wander or totter, at Proverbs 5:6.
roots_lines: Hebrew nua (H5128), to shake, wave, wander, totter, tagged at Pro 5:6.
Webster (1828) spells the word movable.
The Authorized Version keeps the spelling moveable.

The dictionary's move and ponder entries are close kin.

describes the shifting, unmappable path of seduction
set against the God who ponders all a man's goings

etymology: A compound of where and about. Webster (1828) gives the senses “near what place,” “near which place” and “concerning which.”
biblical_def: Whereabout appears once in the Authorized Version, inside a lie. David, fleeing Saul, came alone to the priest at Nob: “Then came David to Nob to Ahimelech the priest: and Ahimelech was afraid at the meeting of David, and said unto him, Why art thou alone, and no man with thee?” (1Sa 21:1). David invented a secret commission: “And David said unto Ahimelech the priest, The king hath commanded me a business, and hath said unto me, Let no man know any thing of the business whereabout I send thee” (1Sa 21:2). There was no business and no royal order. Scripture records the lie without endorsing it, and the next chapter records the cost: Doeg the Edomite saw the meeting and reported it, and Saul had the priests of Nob put to death. David later confessed, “I have occasioned the death of all the persons of thy father's house” (1Sa 22:22). The word is small, but the lesson is not. A lie told to escape danger did not stay contained; it fell on innocent men. “Lying lips are abomination to the LORD: but they that deal truly are his delight” (Pro 12:22).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): WHEREABOUT, near what place; near which place; concerning which.
webster_full: WHEREABOUT, adverb [where and about.]
1. Near what place. Whereabout did you meet your friend?
2. Near which place.
3. Concerning which. The object whereabout they are conversant.
scriptures: And David said unto Ahimelech the priest, The king hath commanded me a business, and hath said unto me, Let no man know any thing of the business whereabout I send thee, and what I have commanded thee: and I have appointed my servants to such and such a place.
Then came David to Nob to Ahimelech the priest: and Ahimelech was afraid at the meeting of David, and said unto him, Why art thou alone, and no man with thee?
Lying lips are abomination to the LORD: but they that deal truly are his delight.
corruption_summary: Narrative passages are mined for moral permission, as though recording a saint's lie meant approving it, when Scripture records David's deception at Nob and then its deadly cost.
corruption_paragraphs: A common shortcut treats Bible stories as examples to copy: if David lied to Ahimelech, a lie in a tight place must be acceptable. That reading confuses description with prescription. Scripture records the sins of its heroes because it is true, not because it approves them, and the law of God, not the conduct of a fugitive, is the rule of life.

The text itself refuses the shortcut. The lie at Nob is followed directly by the slaughter of the priests, and David owns his part in it. The ninth commandment stands over every narrative, and Proverbs 12:22 states the verdict plainly. The one who deals truly is God's delight, even when the truth is costly.
roots_summary: Where plus about; Webster's senses near what place and concerning which; one occurrence, 1 Samuel 21:2.
roots_lines: English compound of where and about.
Webster's third sense, concerning which, is the sense at 1Sa 21:2.
1Sa 21:2 is the only occurrence of whereabout in the Authorized Version.
Doeg the Edomite witnessed the meeting at Nob (1 Samuel 21:7).
1 Samuel 22 records the slaughter of the priests that followed.
usage: the business whereabout I send thee
concerning which: here, an errand that did not exist
a reminder that recorded sins are not approved sins

pos: adv. (as strangers; in a way that misjudges)
etymology: From strange, Old French estrange, Latin extraneus, foreign. Webster (1828) gives as its first sense “with some relation to foreigners.”
biblical_def: Strangely occurs once in the Authorized Version, in the Song of Moses, and the sense is close to Webster's first: acting as foreigners would, misreading what they see. God declares that Israel's rebellion deserved to be ended entirely: “I said, I would scatter them into corners, I would make the remembrance of them to cease from among men” (Deu 32:26). Then He gives the reason He did not: “Were it not that I feared the wrath of the enemy, lest their adversaries should behave themselves strangely, and lest they should say, Our hand is high, and the LORD hath not done all this” (Deu 32:27). The danger was that the nations would misjudge what happened, crediting their own strength for a judgment that came from God and robbing Him of His glory. God preserves His people for the sake of His own name. That is the ground of the church's security: not the worthiness of Israel, nor of any believer, but God's jealousy for His glory, which will not let His enemies boast that they did what only He can do.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): STRANGELY, with some relation to foreigners; wonderfully, in a manner to excite surprise.
webster_full: STRANGELY, adverb 1. With some relation to foreigners.
2. Wonderfully; in a manner or degree to excite surprise or wonder.
How strangely active are the acts of peace.
scriptures: Were it not that I feared the wrath of the enemy, lest their adversaries should behave themselves strangely, and lest they should say, Our hand is high, and the LORD hath not done all this.
I said, I would scatter them into corners, I would make the remembrance of them to cease from among men:
corruption_summary: Man-centred preaching grounds God's faithfulness in the worth of His people, when Deuteronomy 32 grounds it in His zeal for His own name.
corruption_paragraphs: Much popular preaching tells believers that God keeps them because they are valuable to Him in themselves. Deuteronomy 32 gives a sterner and more comforting reason. Israel deserved scattering, and God says so. What spared them was His refusal to let the nations behave themselves strangely and claim His work as their own.

This is the God-centred ground on which the Reformed doctrine of perseverance rests. The saints are kept by the power of God, for the glory of God, and that is far more secure than any confidence in their own worth. The enemy will never be able to say, our hand is high, and the LORD hath not done all this.
roots_summary: From strange, Latin extraneus, foreign; Webster's first sense, with relation to foreigners; one occurrence, Deuteronomy 32:27.
roots_lines: English strangely, from strange, Latin extraneus, foreign.
Webster's first sense: with some relation to foreigners.
Deu 32:27 is the only occurrence of strangely in the Authorized Version.
The verse sits in the Song of Moses, Deuteronomy 32.
God spares His people for the sake of His own name.

the reason God spares His people for His name's sake
